stories.title: Barry Gosin Stepping Down as Newmark’s CEO
stories.excerpt: It’s the end of an era for Newmark. Barry Gosin, the firm’s fearless leader, will step down from his CEO position on Dec. 31, the company announced Friday. Gosin has held the CEO position since 1979. The 75-year-old Gosin will segue to become chairman of Newmark & Company Real Estate, Newmark’s operating company, in order to facilitate a seamless transition for his successor, who will be named by Newmark’s board of directors by year’s end, according to a release. “I have spent nearly my entire career at Newmark, working alongside an exceptional team whose dedication, talent and commitment have made the company and its success possible,” Gosin said in a statement. “The company is stronger than ever, our strategy is working, and the opportunities ahead are substantial, which is why I believe now is the right time to take a step back from day-to-day operations to focus solely on matters that will make a difference to Newmark, and to support the company through this transition.” Stronger than ever is right. At 10,000 professionals over 195 offices, Newmark isn’t the biggest brokerage in the U.S., but that’s intentional. What it is is a lean, mean deal-making machine with a reach that spreads to all corners of the globe — including a 1,000-person team in Europe as well as hubs in Latin America, the Asia-Pacific region, the U.K., Mexico, India and Singapore — and deep expertise in capital markets, leasing, valuation, property management and consulting services across property sectors. Just last month, the firm posted strong results and a robust transaction pipeline in its second-quarter earnings, with Gosin saying Newmark expects double-digit top- and bottom-line growth for the third consecutive year. “We anticipate that our investments in recurring revenue businesses, ongoing international expansion, improving industry fundamentals and talented professionals will together drive Newmark’s long-term growth and market-share gains,” Gosin said during the earnings call. No direct multifamily development impact; brokerage/advisory firm leadership change.
stories.summary: Barry Gosin, who has led Newmark since 1979, will step down as CEO on December 31 and transition to chairman. The firm, which operates 10,000 professionals across 195 offices, will name a successor by year-end. Gosin cited the company's strength and substantial opportunities ahead as reasons for the transition.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Newmark is primarily a brokerage and capital advisory firm; leadership transitions at service providers do not directly affect demand, supply, construction costs, or financing availability for apartment communities.

stories.title: TPG AG, Redfearn Capital Acquire Industrial Portfolio for $628M
stories.excerpt: TPG AG U.S. Real Estate and Redfearn Capital have acquired a 5.4 million-square-foot industrial portfolio for $628 million, Commercial Observer can first report. The seller was DRA Advisors, while BDT & MSD Partners provided a $479 million loan in the deal, sources said. The 53-building portfolio, which is roughly 87 percent occupied, includes both logistics and manufacturing properties spread across Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Minnesota, Illinois and Oregon. Shallow-bay industrial assets in high barrier-to-entry markets make up the majority of the portfolio, and TPG AG now plans to add value through capital investment in the properties. The majority of the portfolio assets are in major industrial markets in the Southeast such as Tampa, Atlanta and Charlotte, N.C. In addition to Redfearn, TPG AG purchased the portfolio with two additional operating partners: Atlanta Property Group and Matterhorn Venture Partners. Each will co-manage the portfolio in their respective markets. “This acquisition represents another significant milestone in our investment strategy and reinforces our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the U.S. shallow-bay industrial sector,” Chris Oka, a managing director at TPG AG, said. “We are pleased to continue our long- standing partnerships with best-in-class operating partners Redfearn, Atlanta Property Group and Matterhorn Venture Partners to acquire and operate a portfolio of high-quality assets with strong occupancy, diversified tenancy, and compelling opportunities to create value through active asset management. We look forward to supporting the portfolio’s continued growth.” “We’ve been intentionally building an industrial platform centered on well-located infill assets in markets with long-term demand,” Alex Redfearn, founder, president and CEO of Redfearn Capital, said in a statement. “This transaction accelerates that strategy in a meaningful way. bullets: TPG AG, Redfearn Capital acquire 5.4M-sf industrial portfolio for $628M from DRA Advisors.

stories.summary: TPG AG U.S. Real Estate and Redfearn Capital acquired a 5.4 million-square-foot, 53-building industrial portfolio for $628 million, with financing of $479 million from BDT & MSD Partners. The portfolio is 87% occupied and spread across seven states, with the majority located in high-barrier-to-entry Southeast markets including Tampa, Atlanta, and Charlotte. TPG plans capital investment to add value to the shallow-bay logistics and manufacturing assets.
stories.impact: This signals strong capital appetite for industrial in high-growth Southeast corridors, particularly Tampa, Atlanta, and Charlotte—markets also experiencing multifamily demand. The $628M deal confirms investor confidence in these Sun Belt logistics hubs, which typically correlate with population in-migration and job growth that strengthen apartment fundamentals. Capital deployed here may compete with development financing in overlapping metros.

stories.title: The New Role of Transitional Debt in Commercial Real Estate Finance
stories.excerpt: Transitional lending was once viewed as a temporary financing solution. Today, it’s becoming a core strategy for life insurers as banks continue moving out of commercial real estate lending, according to a new report from Nuveen. The report said that lower property valuations, tighter banking regulations and a wave of loan maturities are changing the landscape of commercial real estate financing. As banks reduce their exposure, private credit funds and life insurance companies are stepping in to provide capital to borrowers seeking to bridge the gap between traditional mortgage financing and opportunistic debt. Three Structural Shifts Driving the Market Nuveen identified three long-term trends supporting transitional lending. Banks are changing roles. Following the Great Financial Crisis, banks were the main providers of transitional CRE loans. Today, stricter capital and regulatory requirements have made those loans less attractive to hold on bank balance sheets. Rather than originating loans directly, many banks now provide warehouse financing and back leverage to private credit funds, allowing those lenders to originate loans while limiting the banks’ direct CRE exposure. Property values have reset. The rapid increase in rates disrupted commercial real estate valuations for a time. But Nuveen said that several years of transactions have led to more realistic pricing. The result is a lending environment with lower appraised values, tighter covenant loan structures, and spreads of roughly 25 to 40 basis points above prior-cycle averages. As a result, returns are driven more by the economics of the underlying loan than by financial leverage, creating what the report describes as a more durable risk-return profile. The maturity wall remains. A large share of commercial real estate loans originated during the close-to-zero-interest era are coming due. bullets: Life insurers, private credit funds replace banks as primary CRE transitional lenders.
Banks face stricter capital/regulatory requirements; shift to warehouse financing and back leverage roles.
Property valuations reset post-rate shock; transitional lending now core strategy, not temporary solution.
stories.summary: Following tighter banking regulations and property valuation resets post-rate shock, life insurance companies and private credit funds are becoming primary sources of transitional CRE financing, while banks reduce direct exposure and instead provide warehouse financing and back leverage. Transitional lending, once viewed as temporary, is now a core long-term strategy as borrowers bridge the gap between traditional mortgages and opportunistic debt.
stories.impact: Critical for multifamily developers: non-bank lenders (life insurers, credit funds) will dominate construction and bridge financing for apartment projects. Borrowing terms, pricing, and availability will now depend on these alternative sources rather than traditional bank lending. Developers should expect higher spreads, shorter terms, and stronger equity requirements from private lenders; this favors larger, well-capitalized sponsors and may slow development velocity for smaller operators.

stories.title: The Forces Impacting CRE as AI, Energy and Supply Constraints Take Hold
stories.excerpt: When JLL introduced its six forces reshaping global commercial real estate in late 2025, the 2026 outlook was relatively optimistic. The forecast suggested renewed momentum supported by shrinking supply pipelines, economic growth, easing trade concerns, moderating inflation and lower interest rates. Six months later, things have greatly changed. The Middle East conflict, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and continued trade tensions mean global market uncertainties. “For now, we expect somewhat lower growth, higher inflation, and a change of direction in interest rates from what we were anticipating at the start of the year, and that these effects prove temporary and reversible,” JLL said in its recently released “Global Real Estate Outlook Mid-Year, Updated” report. JLL said six structural forces continue to shape international CRE markets. Cost Management as a Strategic Priority Controlling costs was never in doubt. However, energy, commodity and freight disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts elevated cost management from a priority to a primary business driver for corporate leaders. Higher fuel, materials and logistics costs are impacting operating budgets, increasing construction expenses, raising fit-out costs and slowing project timelines. JLL noted that the strategies companies are using to manage costs have not changed. But the urgency behind those efforts has increased. Supply Constraints Create New Opportunities Development pipelines were already shrinking across many property sectors in mature markets. Rising construction costs and uncertainty around project feasibility could limit additional starts. JLL expects well-located secondary assets to benefit from demand spillover, particularly in markets with limited available space. The environment could also create additional opportunities for owners to retrofit and reposition existing properties rather than pursue new construction. bullets: Middle East conflict, Strait of Hormuz closure, trade tensions drive inflation, interest rate uncertainty.
Energy, commodity, freight disruptions elevate cost management to primary business driver for corporates.
Higher fuel, materials, logistics costs impact construction budgets, fit-out expenses, and project timelines.
stories.summary: JLL's mid-year 2026 update revises its January outlook downward due to Middle East conflict, closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and continued trade tensions. The firm now expects lower growth, higher inflation, and interest rate uncertainty. Energy, commodity, and freight disruptions are forcing cost control to become a primary business driver, with direct impacts on construction expenses, fit-out costs, and project timelines.
stories.impact: Multifamily developers face immediate cost inflation risk: construction materials, labor, and logistics are rising due to geopolitical supply-chain disruptions. Project timelines will lengthen, hurting time-to-stabilization and increasing carrying costs. Developers should lock in hard bids and material prices now; those with flexibility in entitlements may consider delaying starts until supply-chain costs stabilize. Inflation also pressures construction lending availability and cap rates, making underwriting tighter.

stories.title: Q2: U.S. Industrial Market Moves Toward Balance as Demand Outpaces New Supply
stories.excerpt: The U.S. industrial market showed signs of stabilization in the second quarter of 2026, with demand beginning to outpace new deliveries while developers remained disciplined about adding new supply. Quarterly reports from CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Lee & Associates discuss a sector that is moving beyond the oversupply concerns of the past two years. Vacancy Stabilizes, Demand Improves After steadily increasing for the past several quarters, the national industrial vacancy rate stabilized in Q2. Increased demand for larger warehouse and distribution facilities helped vacancy decline from its late 2024 peak. At the same time, shallow-bay industrial product experienced a modest increase in vacancy, although availability remains relatively tight compared with historical levels. Absorption Outpaces Deliveries For the first time in several quarters, industrial demand outpaced new deliveries, suggesting a market moving closer to equilibrium. Leasing activity also expanded beyond pre-committed space, as tenants absorbed recently completed speculative projects at a faster pace. Third-party logistics providers remained the largest source of industrial leasing activity during the first half of 2026, while manufacturers also contributed to demand growth. Meanwhile, leasing from general retailers and wholesalers declined as more companies continued to outsource their distribution operations to third parties. Developers Maintain Discipline Although the industrial construction pipeline has increased over the past year, development activity has become less frantic and more reasonable, relative to the recent boom cycle. Much of the space currently under construction consists of build-to-suit projects and larger speculative developments of 200,000 square feet or more. bullets: U.S. industrial vacancy stabilizes in Q2 2026; demand outpaces new deliveries for first time in quarters.
Larger warehouse/distribution demand drives vacancy decline from late 2024 peak; shallow-bay vacancy edges up modestly.
Third-party logistics providers, manufacturers drive leasing; speculative projects absorbed faster than pre-pandemic norms.
stories.summary: The U.S. industrial market showed signs of stabilization in Q2 2026, with demand beginning to outpace new deliveries for the first time in several quarters. The national industrial vacancy rate stabilized after steadily increasing; larger warehouse and distribution demand helped drive vacancy down from its late 2024 peak, though shallow-bay product saw modest vacancy increases. Third-party logistics providers and manufacturers were the primary sources of leasing activity.
stories.impact: While this is positive for industrial, it signals a bifurcated market: large-format logistics assets are tight and in demand, while traditional shallow-bay supply remains soft. Multifamily developers should note that strong logistics leasing in Sun Belt metros (Atlanta, Charlotte, Tampa) reinforces population and job growth trends in those regions, supporting apartment demand. However, note that industrial discipline (fewer starts) reflects broader CRE caution; multifamily should also expect disciplined supply in competitive markets.

stories.title: Fintech Firm More Than Doubles Footprint at 10 Astor Place
stories.excerpt: GFP Real Estate said Thursday that Maybern, a financial technology company specializing in fund management solutions for private markets, has signed a long-term lease expansion at 10 Astor Place, more than doubling its footprint at the property from approximately 11,000 square feet to 30,000 square feet. The expansion encompasses the property’s entire fourth floor. Maybern originally relocated to 10 Astor Place in 2024. Neith Stone of GFP Real Estate represented ownership, alongside Rob Silver, Anthony Sciacca and Brittany Silver of Newmark. Jonathan Franzel and Leo Kone of Newmark represented the tenant. “In today’s market, expansion tells a more meaningful story than relocation,” said Stone.  “When an existing tenant more than doubles its footprint and commits for the long term, it’s a powerful vote of confidence.  Tenants are drawn to boutique buildings like 10 Astor Place because they offer what new construction can’t replicate: enduring architecture, unmatched character and the kind of hands-on ownership today’s companies value.” The post Fintech Firm More Than Doubles Footprint at 10 Astor Place appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Fintech Maybern doubles footprint at 10 Astor Place in Manhattan, 11K to 30K sf, long-term lease.
Expansion occupies entire fourth floor; tenant originally relocated to property in 2024.
Brokers cite expansion (vs. relocation) as vote of confidence; boutique architecture attracts over new construction.
stories.summary: Fintech firm Maybern signed a long-term lease expansion at 10 Astor Place in Manhattan, more than doubling its footprint from approximately 11,000 square feet to 30,000 square feet and occupying the entire fourth floor. The firm originally relocated to the property in 2024. Brokers noted that tenant expansion—rather than relocation—signals confidence, as companies value the building's boutique character and hands-on ownership.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. This is an office lease transaction in Manhattan, not residential. However, it suggests some stabilization in NYC office leasing and fintech tenant confidence, which could support secondary demand for housing in Manhattan neighborhoods; the broader take is that office occupiers are less mobile than feared.

stories.title: Production Fabrication Firm Relocates to Rancho Dominguez
stories.excerpt: DAUM Commercial Real Estate Services completed a 10-year lease agreement for a 35,333 square-foot industrial property at 2945 East Maria St. in Rancho Dominguez on behalf of landlord Crown Associates Realty, Inc. The facility will serve as the West Coast operations hub for Cactus Fabrication, a company specializing in production fabrication for television, film and music videos. The new tenant is relocating from a smaller property in Los Angeles to better accommodate its growing operations, said Chuck Brill, an EVP and principal at DAUM who also serves as co-branch manager of the firm’s South Bay Office. “In addition to providing the larger footprint that the tenant requires, the asset’s quality, heavy electrical capacity, and functional layout featuring a large secured side yard and separate front-loading area is very well suited to their business needs,” Brill said. “Further, ownership has invested significantly in modernizing the building to like-new condition with superior office space, creating a true best-in-class industrial asset that will also act as a tool for attracting employees and creating a strong first impression for customers and business partners.” Hear from the West Coast’s Leading Industrial Real Estate Experts | August 20Gain firsthand insight from the executives, investors, and developers navigating today’s industrial market. From shifting capital flows and debt trends to evolving occupier demand and development strategies, take part in the conversations shaping the future of industrial real estate. bullets: Cactus Fabrication relocates to Rancho Dominguez industrial space, 35.3K sf, 10-year lease.
Tenant moving from smaller LA property to accommodate growth; property features heavy electrical, secured yard.
Crown Associates Realty landlord; DAUM brokered; South Bay industrial market showing tenant expansion/relocation activity.
stories.summary: Cactus Fabrication, a production fabrication company serving television, film, and music video industries, signed a 10-year lease for a 35,333-square-foot industrial facility at 2945 East Maria Street in Rancho Dominguez, serving as the firm's West Coast operations hub. The tenant is relocating from a smaller Los Angeles property to accommodate growth. The landlord, Crown Associates Realty, has modernized the building to best-in-class condition with heavy electrical capacity and functional layout.
stories.impact: South Bay / Rancho Dominguez industrial strength reflects broader Los Angeles region demand for functional, modern warehouse and production space. This signals tenant growth in LA's creative/media economy, which often correlates with millennial and young professional in-migration—a key multifamily demographic. Developers should monitor LA creative districts (Santa Monica, Venice, Silver Lake) for multifamily demand tied to entertainment industry job growth.

stories.title: Mermaid Inn Restaurateurs Ink 2K SF at 61 West 74th Street for New Eatery
stories.excerpt: Restaurateurs Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith are making a splash on the Upper West Side. The couple and co-founders of New England-style seafood spot Mermaid Inn have selected 61 West 74th Street for their next venture, Commercial Observer has learned. Abrams secured the 2,300-square-foot lease, plus a basement space, at $130 per square foot, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. The site, located between Columbus Avenue and Central Park West and about a block and a half south of Mermaid Inn, previously hosted Patsy’s Pizzeria. The locally beloved pizza joint permanently closed in January, citing the end of its lease and rising costs, West Side Rag reported. Counter Real Estate’s Justin Losh negotiated the new lease on behalf of the landlord, Viking Management. Meridian’s Carson Shahrabani and Noam Aziz represented Abrams. “Danny has an iconic restaurant, the Mermaid Inn, right around the corner, so it’s incredible to see him become the LeBron of the immediate neighborhood,” Shahrabani said in a statement to CO. The Upper West Side’s Mermaid Inn set up shop at 335 Columbus Avenue in 2024, after its longtime home along Amsterdam Avenue shuttered in 2022. Abrams and Smith operate a second Mermaid Inn location in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, as well as Mermaid Oyster Bar locations in Greenwich Village and Times Square. The upcoming restaurant at 61 West 74th Street remains unnamed and its concept undecided, according to Shahrabani. Abrams declined to share additional details on the new lease. Losh and Viking Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Mermaid Inn restaurateurs sign 2.3K-sf lease at 61 West 74th St, Manhattan Upper West Side.
Lease at $130/sf; follows Patsy's Pizzeria closure in January citing rising costs and lease end.
Retail spot located between Columbus Ave and Central Park West; existing anchor tenant relocating nearby.
stories.summary: Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith, founders of Mermaid Inn, signed a 2,300-square-foot lease plus basement space at 61 West 74th Street on Manhattan's Upper West Side at $130 per square foot. The location, between Columbus Avenue and Central Park West, previously housed Patsy's Pizzeria, which closed in January due to lease expiration and rising costs. The new venture is positioned one block south of the existing Mermaid Inn location.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily impact. This is a retail lease transaction. However, it signals continued retail challenges on the Upper West Side—Patsy's cited rising costs—which reflects broader NYC commercial real estate pressure but does not directly affect apartment supply, demand, or financing.

stories.title: Nordstrom Rack Takes 22K SF in Wellington, Fla.
stories.excerpt: nordstrom Rack has signed a 22,000-square-foot lease in Wellington, Fla., the Seattle-based retailer announced Thursday. Nordstrom Rack is the discount concept run by Nordstrom. The new store, set to open in spring 2027, will be at The Shoppes at Isla Verde at 800-1020 South State Road 7. Other tenants include Best Buy, Homesense, Total Wine & More, Petco, Old Navy, Ulta and Rack Room Shoes. Terms of the lease were not disclosed. MetLife Investment Management owns the shopping center, while Urban Retail Properties manages the property. MetLife acquired the 207,000-square-foot property in 2018 for $73.75 million, records show. The Shoppes at Isla Verde has experienced some tenant turnover in recent years. A Joann Fabrics store closed in 2025 as that retailer went out of business. According to bankruptcy filings, Joann Fabrics had occupied 21,600 square feet at the plaza since 2008. In another departure, organic grocer Sprouts closed its location at Shoppes at Isla Verde in 2023. Nordstrom Rack sells off-price apparel, accessories, beauty products, home decor and shoes. Nordstrom said it operates 23 Nordstrom Rack stores in Florida. Its Palm Beach County locations include stores in Palm Beach Gardens, West Palm Beach, Delray Beach and Boca Raton. Jeff Ostrowski can be reached at jostrowski@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Nordstrom Rack signs 22K-sf lease in Wellington, FL at The Shoppes at Isla Verde.
Store opens spring 2027; co-tenants include Best Buy, Homesense, Total Wine, Old Navy, Ulta.
Shopping center experienced turnover: Joann Fabrics closed 2025 (21.6K sf), Sprouts closed 2023; MetLife owns property.
stories.summary: Nordstrom Rack, the discount retail concept of Nordstrom, signed a 22,000-square-foot lease in Wellington, Florida at The Shoppes at Isla Verde, scheduled to open in spring 2027. The shopping center is anchored by other tenants including Best Buy, Homesense, Total Wine & More, and Old Navy. The property, owned by MetLife Investment Management, has experienced recent tenant turnover, including the 2025 closure of Joann Fabrics (21,600 sf) and the 2023 closure of Sprouts.
stories.impact: Positive signal for South Florida (Wellington/West Palm Beach area) retail stabilization and consumer spending. Nordstrom Rack's commitment to new openings suggests confidence in population growth and household formation in South Florida markets—demand that also supports multifamily development. Wellington is a growing exurban market with young family and millennial in-migration; retail strength here correlates with apartment demand in and around Palm Beach County.

stories.title: Immigration Law Firm Manifest Law Subleases 18K SF at 902 Broadway
stories.excerpt: The immigration attorneys at Manifest Law will be making some of their own moves, Commercial Observer has learned. The law firm signed a 18,200-square-foot sublease at Koeppel Rosen’s 902 Broadway, where it will be taking over space previously occupied by Adaptive Security, according to tenant brokerage Nomad Group. Asking rent for the space was $75 per square foot. Manifest Law will move into the entire eighth floor nearly four months after the artificial intelligence-powered cybersecurity company firm signed a 51,220-square-foot sublease of its own from BarkBox at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. 902 Broadway spans the length of Broadway between East 20th and East 21st streets, between the landmark Flatiron Building and Union Square. “Manifest’s move underscores Union Square and Flatiron’s emergence as a destination for ambitious AI companies committed to NYC and in-person collaboration,” Nomad’s Bill Janetschek, who represented Manifest Law alongside Nick Hein and Matthew DeRose, said in a statement. “Following its record-setting $60 million Series A, Manifest needed an HQ equal to its trajectory and a team capable of moving at its speed.” Christopher Foerch and Zev Holzman of Savills handled negotiation on behalf of Adaptive Security, but did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Manifest Law is relocating about five blocks from 333 Park Avenue South, according to Nomad Group. Other recent deals signed at 902 Broadway were for law firm Fenwick & West, which expanded to 72,800 square feet across four floors in June, and real estate development firm Hudson Companies taking 18,200 square feet in March. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Immigration law firm Manifest Law subleases 18.2K sf at 902 Broadway (Flatiron), Manhattan.
Tenant takes entire eighth floor after cybersecurity firm Adaptive Security sublet; Manifest raised $60M Series A.
Nomad brokerage notes Union Square/Flatiron emerging as AI company destination for in-person collaboration.
stories.summary: Immigration law firm Manifest Law signed an 18,200-square-foot sublease at 902 Broadway (Flatiron Building area) in Manhattan, occupying the entire eighth floor previously held by AI-powered cybersecurity firm Adaptive Security. Manifest Law recently raised a $60 million Series A and is seeking office space reflective of its growth trajectory and commitment to in-person collaboration in New York City.
stories.impact: Modest positive signal for Manhattan office leasing and tech/AI tenant demand in the Union Square/Flatiron neighborhood, but primarily reflects office sector, not multifamily. However, the continued influx of well-capitalized AI and fintech companies to NYC (Series A rounds, expansions) reinforces job growth in high-wage sectors, supporting rental demand from young professionals in Manhattan and outer-borough multifamily markets.
